title: POC weekly - latency tuning (MontvaleBank)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latency results (TTFT and tail latencies), discuss streaming behavior, sequence length distributions, kernel selection tradeoffs and next tuning steps. Agreed to run another benchmark with streaming enabled and adjusted batch/kv cache settings; Redwood to share kernel-map and updated runbook.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-30 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Liu (Redwood SRE); Emily Rivera (CTO), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML), Sarah Kim (Platform), Jorge Alvarez (Infra)

Summary / Notes (auto-gen may be noisy):
- Quick recap of last week: improved avg token latency 12% with smaller batches; TTFT still high on long prompts for streaming path.
- Action items: run streaming benchmark w/ kv-cache enabled end-to-end, provide kernel-selection mapping, and share config snippet for nginx/ALB timeouts.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jamie: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we got about 45 minutes, we'll go through the numbers you sent and then plan the next bench, sound good?
[00:15] Emily: yep that's great, thanks. quick note — Liam's gonna screen share the dashboard shortly.
[00:22] Liam: yeah i'm pulling the run now — there's a couple of plots, one for p50/p95 and TTFT on streaming and non-streaming.
[00:34] Ravi: cool, before the screen share quick question — for the streaming runs did you use the streaming sdk or are you using chunked responses from the test harness? sometimes the harness does chunking differently and that affects the first byte.
[00:48] Sarah: we used our in-house harness, which basically polls and reassembles chunks. could be that we're adding an extra buffering layer.
[01:05] Liam: ok when i ran the baseline on monday, TTFT for short prompts was 180-220ms, but for longer sequences it shot up to 420ms on average — that's TTFT not total.
[01:20] Maya: 420ms, that sounds like there's an extra compilation or kernel warmup on the streaming path, sometimes the model fallback picks a different kernel for small batch sizes.
[01:36] Jorge: we also saw some spikes aligned with autoscale events — when new pods come up, the first few requests hit cold caches.
[01:50] Jamie: good call — we should separate cold start noise from steady-state. did you pin the model version?
[01:58] Liam: yes pinned, but we were switching between an int8 quant and a fp16 variant during the runs — trying to see cost tradeoffs.
[02:12] Ravi: that switching could explain the kernel change. also for streaming, the runtime may choose a different attention kernel when seq len distribution is wide — our kernel map will show that.
[02:26] Emily: can you explain kernel map? i think some of our infra people misread it last time.
[02:33] Ravi: sure — basically runtime selects a specific compute kernel (e.g., fused-attn-v1, flash-attn-like, or fallback matmul) based on sequence length, batch size and quantization. i'll send the mapping per model so you can see which kernel fired for each bucket.
[02:50] Liam: perfect. ok screen share: here's the dashboard — p50 is looking fine ~12ms per token, p95 jumps especially for sequences >1024.
[03:05] Sarah: we're defaulting max_seq to 2048 in the client, but 80% of our requests are in the 400-600 token range. we still see padding overhead because the model runtime pads to the longest in the batch.
[03:20] Maya: yep, padding on CPU/GPU memory layout can blow up throughput, consider dynamic batching with sequence bucketing; that reduces wasted compute.
[03:34] Jamie: did you try kv-prefix caching for repeated system prompts?
[03:38] Liam: minimal — we have a short system prompt but it's present on most calls, we didn't enable prefix cache because of concerns about memory in the dedicated pool.
[03:48] Ravi: prefix caching (KV cache) will cut TTFT for repeated context a lot; tradeoff is memory. for montvale workload with repeatable system prompts, it's likely worth enabling for the low-latency tier.
[04:05] Jorge: memory pressure is a real concern — we have a tight cap on GPU mem per pod. how much does KV caching add?
[04:12] Ravi: depends on sequence length, but roughly 1-2 bytes per token per KV entry depending on quantization; i'll share a sizing table.
[04:24] Liam: about streaming specifically — we saw cases where streaming TTFT > non-streaming TTFT which is weird because streaming should emit faster.
[04:36] Maya: that often comes from buffering in the client or the LB; confirm keepalives and chunk timeouts.
[04:44] Sarah: nginx default 60s timeouts are fine but chunk thresholds could be delaying first flush. we can lower flush interval.
[04:52] Jamie: redwood also has a per-request chunking buffer threshold — we'll share the recommended streaming config.
[05:00] Emily: ok next, quantization — when you switched to int8 our tail latencies improved but TTFT got worse in some windows?
[05:12] Ravi: int8 reduces compute but sometimes introduces extra dequant/dequantize passes in the runtime which can increase per-request latency for small batches. also some optimized kernels aren't available for certain quant formats.
[05:28] Liam: so kernel availability matters — do you have a list of kernels supported per quant format?
[05:33] Ravi: yes, will send a matrix; e.g., fused-attn-v2 supports fp16 and q4_0, but not qint8 on this runtime version.
[05:44] Jamie: action: provide kernel-matrix and recommended quant profiles for your workload.
[05:50] Sarah: thanks. on batching — we tried raising max_batch to 8 and saw throughput improve but TTFT for single-user flows increased.
[05:59] Maya: that's expected; batching reduces per-token cost but increases time to first token. we can tune adaptive batching: prefer fast path for low concurrency requests and batch during spikes.
[06:14] Jorge: can Redwood do routing by policy? e.g., route low-latency customer calls to a dedicated low-batch pool and background to high-batch.
[06:23] Jamie: yes, smart routing can do per-route policies (latency vs cost) — you can tag routes and set different pools. we'll share an example config.
[06:33] Ravi: another note — the streaming path uses a different IO stack. when we enabled early flushing in previous POC we saw 30% lower TTFT but a few more small packets; recommended to coordinate with your infra team on MTU and keepalive.
[06:48] Liam: can we also replicate the autoscale spikes? we'd like to see the first-token behavior when a new node comes up.
[06:55] Jamie: yes, we can run a cold-start benchmark and a steady-state benchmark. we'll include pod startup timings and kernel warmup traces.
[07:05] Emily: timeline — if we get the next run by next wednesday we can decide on pilot sizing.
[07:11] Jamie: sounds good. we'll target next wednesday.
[07:15] Ravi: quick question from my side — are you using private (VPC) deployment or hosted for this POC?
[07:21] Jorge: VPC with dedicated nodes in our cloud account.
[07:25] Ravi: ok that affects kernel availability sometimes (container runtime, CUDA driver mismatch) — please share driver versions.
[07:32] Liam: we run CUDA 12.2 and a custom NVIDIA driver; i'll paste versions.
[07:38] Maya: note — driver mismatches can force fallback kernels and cause latency spikes. we'll look out for that in the traces.
[07:46] Sarah: any more questions?
[07:49] Emily: no, good recap. thanks everyone.

Recap & Next steps (auto):
- Redwood to share: kernel map + kernel matrix per quant format; streaming config snippet; recommended adaptive batching policy example; sizing table for KV cache memory.
- Customer to run: streaming-enabled benchmark w/ KV cache on vs off; cold-start bench during autoscale; collect driver/kernel logs.
- Schedule: Redwood to deliver artifacts by Tue EOD; next sync Wed 2027-09-07 10:00 PT (tentative).

Transcript end. (note: transcription may have small errors - names or product names slightly off)
